title: A Letter for the Orchard
premise: In 1893, on a storm-battered coast, widowed lighthouse keeper Tamsin Okonkwo has spent seven years keeping her head down and her late husband's papers hidden. When census taker Elias Wren arrives asking questions no census requires, he reveals he is hunting documents that could topple the colonial magistrate who destroyed Tamsin's husband. As the great storms isolate the coast and the river ice begins to break, Tamsin and Elias must smuggle the evidence past three checkpoints, each guarded by someone who once called her friend. The journey costs them allies, forces Tamsin to choose between loyalty to her dead husband's memory and the dangerous truth of what he actually did, and ends at the orchard where it all began—with Tamsin testifying, the magistrate undone, and the lighthouse finally dark by choice rather than fear.
about_author: I. M. Okonkwo is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing colonial-era correspondence before turning to fiction. They write from a small house near the sea, where they claim every storm sounds like an argument worth overhearing.

chapters.title: The Question That Wasn't on the Form
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. During the year's first great storm, census taker Elias Wren arrives soaked and asks, off the record, whether she ever corresponded with a man named Aldous Vane. Tamsin lies smoothly, but after he leaves she digs up her husband's old sea chest. Emotional beat: the past knocking politely before it breaks the door.

chapters.title: What the Sea Chest Kept
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. She reads letters revealing her husband Daniel was gathering testimony against Magistrate Corrigan before his drowning—ruled accidental. The letters name three checkpoints along the river road: the ferry, the garrison, the customs house. Emotional beat: grief curdling into purpose.

chapters.title: A Keeper's Routine
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Wren returns under pretense of correcting the census, probing gently. We learn he lost his sister to one of Corrigan's courts and has spent years building a case that needs Daniel's final ledger. Emotional beat: two liars recognizing each other's craft.

chapters.title: The Orchard in Winter
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. She visits the abandoned orchard where Daniel hid the ledger beneath a graft-marked apple tree, retrieving it as the second storm hits. Her neighbor Marta sees her and says nothing—but will remember. Emotional beat: touching the past and finding it heavier than expected.

chapters.title: Marta's Silence Has a Price
chapters.summary: Marta's POV. Marta weighs loyalty to Tamsin against her son's post at the ferry checkpoint, which Corrigan controls through debt. She warns Tamsin obliquely over bread and salt. Emotional beat: friendship strained across a widening crack.

chapters.title: Ledger of Small Crimes
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Reading the ledger fully, she discovers Daniel took bribes early on before turning witness—the truth is not clean, and neither was he. Elias argues the corruption matters more than the man; Tamsin disagrees. Emotional beat: memory as contested ground.

chapters.title: Ice on the River Road
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. The plan forms: move the ledger downstream before the ice breaks and the spring court convenes, using the last legal ferry crossing. Corrigan's men are already asking about strangers on the coast. Emotional beat: the clock starting.

chapters.title: First Checkpoint: The Ferryman
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Disguised as a widow shipping fruit crates from the orchard, she crosses at the ferry where Marta's son Tobiah works. He recognizes her crate markings and lets her pass—but takes one apple as proof he could have stopped her. Emotional beat: mercy with teeth.

chapters.title: Corrigan Comes Calling
chapters.summary: Magistrate Corrigan's POV. Charming and rotting, Corrigan visits the lighthouse under flag of courtesy, praising Tamsin's service while letting slip he knows Daniel kept records. He offers her a pension for silence. Emotional beat: power wearing its most reasonable face.

chapters.title: The Refusal
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Alone after Corrigan leaves, Tamsin nearly burns the ledger—loyalty to Daniel's shame warring with duty to his victims. She remembers the drowned boy from the trial records and rekindles the lamp instead. Emotional beat: choosing truth over comfortable forgetting.

chapters.title: Storm Between Us
chapters.summary: Dual POV. The third and greatest storm strands Elias at the lighthouse; trapped together for three days, they argue about whether exposing Daniel's bribes destroys the cause or purifies it. A fragile trust forms. Emotional beat: intimacy forged in confinement.

chapters.title: Tobiah's Dilemma
chapters.summary: Tobiah's POV. Corrigan's clerk interrogates Tobiah about the widow with the fruit crates. Tobiah lies badly, then well, realizing he has crossed a line he cannot uncross. He sends a coded warning downstream. Emotional beat: a small man discovering his own spine.

chapters.title: Second Checkpoint: The Garrison
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. At the garrison checkpoint, Sergeant Hale—an old comrade of Daniel's—must choose between the uniform that feeds him and the man who once saved his life. He delays the search until the courier sledge passes. Emotional beat: loyalty bending without breaking.

chapters.title: Betrayal at the Customs House Gate
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. The third checkpoint falls differently: customs officer Brandt, bought long ago, seizes the decoy crate and arrests their hired courier. Elias escapes into the marshes with nothing but knowledge that Corrigan now expects the real ledger. Emotional beat: the plan bleeding out.

chapters.title: What Was Lost Was Never There
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. News reaches the lighthouse that the courier talked. Tamsin realizes the seized crate held only apples—and that she never told anyone the ledger's true hiding place, because she only just remembered it herself: inside the lighthouse lamp room, in Daniel's old logbook binding. Emotional beat: terror and grim relief entwined.

chapters.title: The Lamp Room Confession
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. She finds Daniel's confession sewn into the logbook—he caused the drowning of a witness, not just took bribes. Loyalty to his memory shatters against the truth. She decides the whole record must go forward, damning parts included. Emotional beat: mourning a man she never truly knew.

chapters.title: Last Crossing Before the Break
chapters.summary: Dual POV. With the ice groaning apart, Tamsin and Elias make the river crossing themselves, pursued by Brandt's riders. Tobiah holds the ferry an extra minute against orders; Marta stands on the bank as visible witness so no one dares shoot. Emotional beat: a community quietly conspiring.

chapters.title: Third Checkpoint: The Ice Bridge
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The road ends; the only way forward is across the cracking ice to the courthouse landing. Brandt catches them at the edge. Elias stalls him with words while Tamsin walks the ice alone, ledger strapped to her chest. Emotional beat: courage as a solitary arithmetic.

chapters.title: The Reading of the Ledger
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. In the spring court, the ledger is read aloud—bribes, drownings, Corrigan's signature trail. Corrigan's defense collapses when Hale testifies and Tobiah produces the apple and the ferry manifest. Emotional beat: quiet words doing loud work.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Called to the stand, Tamsin tells all of it—including Daniel's crimes—refusing to let love edit the record. The courtroom's silence breaks into something like respect. Emotional beat: truth spoken whole, at last, in her own voice.

chapters.title: After the Verdict
chapters.summary: Marta's POV. Corrigan is remanded; the town absorbs the fallout. Marta buries the year's grievances with the winter, and she and Tamsin plant new stock in the orchard from the surviving grafts. Emotional beat: ordinary life resuming as its own kind of victory.

chapters.title: A Letter for the Orchard
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tamsin writes a letter to Daniel and buries it beneath the graft tree—not forgiveness, not blame, just the truth delivered home. She extinguishes the lighthouse lamp for the season and sleeps without dreaming of storms. Emotional beat: memory laid down like a tool after the work is done.
